sentences.text: Dinheirosaurus is estimated to have reached a length of 20 to 25 meters and weighed approximately 8.8 metric tons.
A 1.05-meter-long footprint found near Dinheirosaurus fossils suggests the genus may have been even larger than current estimates.
Only two cervical vertebrae are preserved from the Dinheirosaurus holotype, despite the animal likely having fifteen.
The preserved fourteenth cervical vertebra has a centrum length of 63 cm and is well-preserved with a concave bottom edge.
Dinheirosaurus is one of the few sauropods known to have gastroliths found alongside its type specimen.
Dinheirosaurus lourinhanensis was first described by José Bonaparte and Octávio Mateus in 1999 based on fossils from the Lourinhã Formation.
The holotype specimen of Dinheirosaurus, catalogued as ML 414, was discovered in 1987 by Carlos Anunciação.
Dinheirosaurus likely possessed a whip-like tail, a characteristic feature of diplodocids.
Dinheirosaurus was likely a non-selective ground feeder.
Research suggests Dinheirosaurus likely used gastroliths to absorb minerals rather than for an avian-style gastric mill, as its gastrolith mass was far lower than the 1.05% typical of birds.
A 2012 study by Mannion et al. classified Dinheirosaurus as the sister species to Supersaurus vivianae, forming the most basal group of diplodocines.
In 2015, Dinheirosaurus lourinhanensis was reclassified as a species of Supersaurus, becoming Supersaurus lourinhanensis.
Dinheirosaurus lived during the early Tithonian stage of the Late Jurassic period, while other estimates place it in the Kimmeridgian stage, approximately 152.21 to 149.2 million years ago.
Dinheirosaurus is one of many eusauropods found in the Late Jurassic of Europe.

A 2014 cladogram suggested that Dinheirosaurus was more primitive than Apatosaurus and placed it outside the subfamily Diplodocinae.
